newsitem.title: USA: United States sending election experts to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: United States sending election experts to Bosnia.

text.p: A day after Defence Secretary William Cohen sharply criticised a new delay in Bosnia's municipal elections, the United States on Friday announced plans to send experts to the Balkan country to prepare for the polls.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said 33 U.S. election registration supervisors will leave for Bosnia on Sunday and another 100 Americans would follow shortly after.
"We believe it's important to get supervisors and trainers on the ground now to prepare for these elections which will be held next September," he told reporters.
The group will work with local election commissions in Bosnia to make sure the process of registering voters in all the municipalities complies with international standards.
Washington will also contribute 10 members to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation permanent staff office in Sarajevo to run the elections next September.
Also, Burns insisted Washington was unified in backing a delay in Bosnia's municipal elections despite Defence Secretary William Cohen's sharp criticism of the postponment.
Burns said it would be "holding him (Cohen) to a standard that is too high" to expect Cohen to give the same full answer to an issue like the polls delay as other government entities.

But other officials said State Department authorities were annoyed by Cohen's criticism of the delay. The decision was made by the OSCE on the recommendation of American Robert Frowick, who is overseeing the elections process for the OSCE.
Cohen, in Bosnia, called the delay another failure by outside civilian agencies to rejuvenate the war-shattered country.

"I can only say it is disappointing. It will complicate matters," he told a news conference. "I am disappointed with those who are responsible for setting up and acquiring the (election) monitors, the financial resources in order to allow the elections to go forward."

In Washington Burns said: "It's always disappointing when you have to postpone elections, but this is only a two-month postponement and we believe the postponement will give us a greater chance to have free and fair elections."
"We thought carefully about his (Frowick's) reasoning and we support him fully in this assessment," Burns added.
Despite the conflict, Burns said on Friday: "I know we have a unified government this morning on this (elections) issue."

Asked if he would have preferred Cohen to declare full support for the delay, Burns said: "I think you're holding him to a standard that is too high ... If I give an answer here ... on an issue that we've talked about, and I just say one point, and I don't give you all my auxiliary points, does that mean that I've failed in my job? I don't think so."
U.S. officials told Reuters the Pentagon was given a copy in advance of Burns' Thursday guidance on the elections issue.

Cohen's predecessor, William Perry, was often more frank in public than other officials and influenced policy in this way. Since taking office in January, however, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright made it clear she wants to reassert her department's pre-eminence on foreign policy issues.
U.S. officials said Cohen's comments reflected concern the postponement would require the Pentagon to make unspecified adjustments in its plans for withdrawing troops from Bosnia.
Cohen, speaking on Thursday in Bosnia, however, reiterated the U.S. intention to withdraw it troops from Bosnia by mid-1998 and Burns said on Friday that remains U.S. policy.

"... When we made the decision late last autumn to commit American troops to the (newest phase of the Bosnia military) operation, it was done in the clear understanding with our European allies and the other contributing nations that we would be there for about 18 months. And that clock started two months ago," Burns said.

The local polls were originally to be in September 1996, along with general elections, but were postponed because of widespread election fraud over refugee registration to November 1996 and then to July this year. Western countries funding the election pushed to delay the vote further to allow more time to organise refugee registration and international monitoring. Burns on Friday said again he expects no more delays.
